The government are on the air, I might say, only about once in six weeks and I know the western members can verify what I have just said.

I should like to refer to
some remarks I made last session with regard to a radio licence that was granted in ithe city of Windsor to the station known as CKOK. Preliminary to what I have to say, I should like to mention again certain principles which were laid down by the Prime Minister when he introduced the radio bill, namely, that two of the purposes of having a radio commission were to ensure that radio stations located should be under Canadian control, and also that programs broadcast in Canada should be of Canadian origin, using Canadian material and fostering a Canadian spirit, if I might put it in that way.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
If my hon. friend
will permit me, would he have any objection to postponing his remarks on this question until the hon. member for East Essex is present? He is away this evening, and he asked me to bring up this matter when he was here.

I may not be here when he is here. I have no particular objection to the minister's request, but last year when I made my statement the hon. member for East Essex was not in the house, and when he made his statement I was not ini the house1. However, I am quite willing to agree to the minister's suggestion, but I should like to know when the matter is coming up again because I want to speak on it.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Any time my hon.
friend wishes, except this evening if he will agree to postpone his remarks.

It is not particularly serious. My hon. friend from East Essex, for whom I have every regard and respect, can very readily answer my remarks to-morrow if I continue now. May I add that the member who should reply to what I have to say is the minister himself, and not the member for East Essex?
Last year when I brought this matter up I made the statement in the presence of the Prime Minister that the station at Windsor was controlled by Americans, not by Canadians, and that it was really created, in my opinion, for the use of the city of Detroit; that the United States people who are really behind the granting of that licence could not themselves obtain a licence in the city of Detroit, and therefore they sought a Canadian licence in order to serve that large territory, the city of Detroit. They got the licence. I made that statement, and on the following day, when I chanced not to be present in the house, the Minister of Marine made the following statement, at page 3432 of Hansard of May 25, 1932:
As far as the department is aware, the company is a bona fide Canadian company and is under Canadian control.
The minister goes on to say with reference to the statement that had been made that the station was under the control of the Columbia Broadcasting Company, and that the Columbia Broadcasting Company had a similar arrangement with other Canadian stations. He cited the Rogers-Majestic and Gooderham and Worts in Toronto and the Canadian Marconi Company and La Presse in Montreal, and then he said:
As far as the department is aware there is nothing happening as was stated by the hon. member for North Waterloo.
I must take that to be a direct denial, if you like, of the statement that the company was under United States control and that the greater portion of its programs was of United States origin. The minister further stated:
If it was brought to the attention of the department that practically the whole time of this

Supply-Marine-Radio
station was being leased to American companies for the advertising of American goods in Canada, the department would take the necessary steps to see that such a practice did not continue.
I have no desire to injure any Canadian investment, and it may be that now this company is more largely under Canadian control than it was last year. But I do want to submit for the information of the minister, if he does not know' it, and certainly for the information of the committee, that this is a United States station, or was as late as last June, and controlled by United States people.
1 have here a price list issued by the Columbia Broadcasting system. They have a list of twenty-two cities, the basic network it is called, and among these stations are listed Detroit, Windsor. It does not even pay the compliment to the Canadian station of naming Windsor first. There are twenty-two stations listed here, only one of which is Canadian. There are n>o Toronto or Montreal stations listed as being in the basic network of the Columbia Broadcasting system of the United States.
I can give a little more proof as to the ownership of the station itself. I have before me sw'orn evidence given before the Federal Radio Commission of the United States, sitting in Washington, and I shall quote just sufficient from the evidence to prove what I have said. The question was asked:
What part of the stock of the Essex Broadcasters

Those are the owners of the station at Windsor:

does the Fort Industry Oil Company own? Does it own a controlling interest in the Essex Broadcasters Limited?
A. I will answer that in this way, that the exact amount is not determined, but it is a controlling interest.
The question was repeated:
Q. Is it a controlling interest?
A. Yes.
That is from the sworn evidence given before the Federal Radio Commission of the United States.
What is the date of that?

June 18, 1932. The investigation was held at Washington. My remarks of last year were made prior to the taking of this evidence, so I submit that at that time my statement was absolutely correct. It may be, and I am so informed by some Canadians who are interested in this station, and whose investment I do not desire to injure, that some change has taken place. The statement was made to me a few days ago that now 51 per cent of the stock is held in

Canada. Whether that is so or not, I have no means of knowing. This, however, is true, that the other principle which was supposed to be observed is being violated; that is, that the greater proportion, in fact ninety per cent or more, of all the broadcasting, advertising and otherwise, that is done over that station, comes from United States sources. It does seem to me, and I say this in all kindness so far as the Canadians who are interested in this station are concerned, that that is not in accordance with the spirit of the creation of the Canadian radio commission. I said that ninety per cent of the broadcasting was of United States origin. I will give a few figures. I have a detailed record of the broadcasting from June 1 to June 8, 1932. It shows that ninety-four per cent of the time that CKOK was on the air in that period was used either by Columbia or Detroit. Anything that is broadcast by Columbia emanates I think from the city of New York. There were 192 announcements-I am referring to advertising alone-for Detroit merchants and 57 announcements for Canadian merchants. I have here the record of another week of broadcasting and the proportion is just about the same.
I would like to know if the minister can tell me whether the conditions as outlined here and as stated by me last year, and as they apparently existed in July of last year, still obtain. I hesitate to say to him that if he finds the facts are as stated he should cancel that licence. I know it is given as a reason or an excuse why American capital is interested in this station, that Canadian capital could not have been obtained. It is stated as a reason that the station had to take American advertising and American programs because they could not obtain them in Canada. I believe that is the fact. There has been a very large sum of money expended in that Windsor station, upwards of $200,000, and naturally the men who 'have invested their money in it are trying to get a return on their investment.
It was stated to me the other day by one who is interested in that station that it was quite impossible to get Canadian advertiser's to contract for tire time, and for that reason they had to accept United States programs. It was also stated theut when those contracts expire Canadians could get on the air and make contracts in place of the United States citizens. But I doubt very much if they will ait anj' time find enough Canadian business in the city of Windsor, important as it is, to take up the majority of the time of that station. The point I wish particularly to make, is that we aue not observing the prin-

Supply-Marine-Radio
ciples laid down when the radio commission was formed', which stipulated not only that the companies should remain under Canadian control, buit thait thait whidh they broadcast should be of Canadian origin and for the benefit of Canadian people. I should like, if possible, to have some infarmaitdon from the minister. This is one out of only thirteen Canadian cheunmels. Last year we obtained more exclusive channels, and were very glad to get them. The channel dim question is exclusively used by this concern, and it seems a pity to me that omie of the channels so hand won by the Canadian' people should be allocated almost entirely for the benefit of the people of another country. That is the point I wish to make, and if possible I should like to have same reassurance from the minister that the condition' is bettor than that I outlined last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: When the hon. member raised the same point last year the company in question was not in operation. The licence had been issued, but they were not operating. My information is that the com-pamy began operating on June 1, 1932.
I spoke in May.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Yes, I believe that is correct. I do not know the exact conditions under which they operated lost fall, but I can say to the bouse that to-day the management is entirely in the hands of Canadians. More than fifty-one per oent of the capital is owned by Canadians, and all the directors are Canadians.
That does not mean very much.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: There is one director from Sandwich, one from Windsor, one from Walkerviile, one from Essex, one from Teeum-seh and the remaining two from Windsor. Them is no doubt that at the present time the management is in the hands of Canadians. Of course this broadcasting station, as all other Canadian stations, depends on advertising for its revenue, and as I said last year, so long as the stations operate' on the presept basis, one cannot readily see a reason why a Canadian station should not rent a certain amount of its time-
Yes, a certain amount of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
-to United States advertisers, provided, of course, that no Cam-adnam programs are offering.
Mr*. EULER: Would the minister say that if a Canadian advertiser wanted to get time now he could get it?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Yes, I think so.
If they are under contract with Americans?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I think so.
Can the minister tell us how many purely Canadian programs ever issue from that station?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I cannot give that information now, but I can say to the hon. member and the committee that for some time my department have been following the operations of that station, and I frankly admit thait we are not altogether satisfied with it. We believe that the station is giving an undue proportion of its time to American programs. If the control of radio stations had remained under the jurisdiction of my department it was the intention of the minister and the department to exercise more control over the company at Windsor. We had even thought of putting some conditions into effect when we renewed the licence for this year.
Is not the commission itself under the control and regulation of the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Since the radio commission has been in operation the station has come under its control.
But is the commission not under the control of the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: To some extent, yes; they have to report to me. I have to be their spokesman in this house. But the commission has control over stations. I can say that the station in Windsor is carefully looked after by the radio commission, and I think thait within a short time it will see that the station is operating according to law.
Is there another station at Windsor?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: No, that is the only one.
May I suggest that the minister should give the station in Windsor to the Border Cities Star, a very good paper. The minister could do in Windsor what he has done in Montreal.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I do not think the hon. member can compare the city of Windsor with the city of Montreal.
No, but I can compare the Border Cities Star with La Patrie.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
The hon. member for North Waterloo said' a moment ago that
Supply-Marine-Radio

the Windsor station, because of the small size of the city could not get sufficient Canadian programs to employ all its time in broadcasting. I believe one station is enough for that city. I think however the committee may rest assured that the radio commission will look into the matter and give satisfaction.
My point of comparison is that the Border Cities Star and La Patrie may both be newspapers, but the Border Cities Star is a prominent newspaper.

I understand that the station in Detroit, to which we are referring, began operations in June.
An lion. MEMBER: Windsor.

No, Detroit; why not
be fair about if? That is where it is operated from. I am informed upon good authority that seventy-five per cent of the broadcasting from that station is done from a Detroit studio. I understand from an employee of the station that the Windsor station is looked upon merely as a blind.
A blind pig.
Bootlegging radio.

No, there are lots of those in Detroit-or at least there were, anyway. In my opinion this should be a Canadian station. I do not believe we should be merely a convenience at a time when channels on the other side of the boundary line become crowded. We should not permit the very few channels at our disposal to be used for that extra advertising. Those channels should be used for the benefit of the Canadian people. In my view that was the fundamental principle underlying the appointment of the commission in Canada. I do not believe it was ever intended that licence should be granted to a station which had for its chief purpose the dissemination of American advertising. I am not unmindful of the fact that possibly there i>
more financial gain in the broadcasting of American advertising. However I do not believe there is a great deal of excuse for the conditions which have obtained at Windsor. The station commenced operations in June and the radio commission did not begin its work until October. From June until October they operated with 75 per cent of the material emanating from a studio in Detroit and 25 per oent from a studio in Windsor. If it is to be an American station why not change the call and be frank about it? If it is to be a Canadian station it should be Canadian. I have no sympathy with the people who invested money under those conditions.
[Mr. Duranleau.l

Has the commission arrived at the point of putting in force the regulation that only five per cent of the time shall be devoted to advertising? Because I am quite certain that this station is not observing that regulation. Perhaps others are not either.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
As my hon. friend
knows, it was only in January that the technical member of the radio commission returned from England, where he was studying broadcasting operations, and, as stated this evening, he was not sworn in until, I think, the 15th or 16t.h of January. I could not say exactly how far the commission is exercising control of Canadian stations as to the five per cent of the time mentioned by my hon. friend. But I know it is preparing to enforce the law. This committee will permit me to add that personally I am of the opinion-and I will discuss the matter with the radio commission, -that the foreign programs handled by any Canadian station should be limited to programs advertising goods actually manufactured in Canada and to non-advertising programs of high quality. That is the view of the minister and of the department, I hope the radio commission will accept and enforce that view even in connection with the broadcasting station at Windsor.

I heard the
Minister of Marine say he was not satisfied with the operation of that station. May I ask if he reported the case to the radio commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Oh yes, my information is that the case of that station is in the hands of and under consideration by the commission at the present time.

Has a new licence been
issued?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: The licence will not be renewed before the first of April; they come for renewal on that date. As I told the committee a minute ago, probably some restrictions or conditions will be imposed on that station before the licence is renewed.
' The first of April? Make it the second.

I think the hon. member for East Hamilton put his finger on the important feature, that is the division of air channels as between the United States and Canada. After all, in spite of the enormous amount of air, the available air channels are limited, and in the division between the two countries I understand that the air channels which Canada may use are comparatively

Supply-Marine-Radio
few. The arrangement between ourselves and the United States being what it is, the duty of our commission is to see to it that Canada does get her proper share of those channels. Undoubtedly, if the station at Windsor is being used as is stated, the effect is simply a detraction from the limited number of channels allotted to Canada, and an addition to those available to the United States.
I made a very interesting discovery the other day. I got a radio for the first time. I had always been under the impression that the tariffs of this country were sufficiently high to keep out anything American, or almost so. But to my amazement I found that at least three quarters of the programs sent out by a radio outfit in Alberta were American programs. I suggest to the minister that he confer with the Prime Minister and with the Minister of National Revenue and make certain whether or not there is a gap in their tariff wall.

May I, with some reluctance, but in the interest of my hon. friend the minister and his party, make one other suggestion? It is that since the president of this particular station at Windsor happens to be the president of the Conservative association, he be very particular to see that the regulations are carried out, lest he be accused of favoritism.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Well the radio commission is a non-political commission.

Is the minister smiling?
And hon. MEMBER: Yes he is.
I would like to ask, for my own informationi and the information of the house, and .perhaps of the country: Is the new radio commission under the control and jurisdiction of the Department of Marine?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: As I have already stated, the radio commission has to report to the Minister of Marine.
And vice versa?

Mr. Chairman, that is an answer, but I do not think it means much. I should like to press my question, because I regard it as important. A great deal of money will be spent on this radio commission; what service will they render, and to whom will they be responsible? Does the minister consider that he is really the chief of that commission? Or does the chairman of the commission report to him? Are they under his control, or are they under their own control?
Or is the commission responsible to the people, or to the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation?
I think perhaps this is an opportune time for the minister to make a frank admission in regard to the whole broadcasting situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: There is no admission to be made dn the part of the minister.
He never admits.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: The act is there, and there are a number of great lawyers on the other side of the house-my hon. friend from Quebec East could say better than myself. The act is short; it comprises only five or six pages, and one has only to read it to see whether the commission is under the control of the minister or not.
That is altogether too guileless.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: To some extent I think I can say that the commission is under the control of the minister-if you can say, for instance, that the railway commission is under the control of the Minister of Railways. The radio commission is a commission that has certain powers.
Is it a court?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: No, it is not a court.
That is why it is different.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: But the commission has administrative powers; the only requirement is that they report to the minister once a year.

I am mot yet through with my question. With all due deference to the minister I must say that I am not any wiser now than, before I asked the question, I will put the question in another way. The minister says he does not really know whether he is in control or not-

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: No, I do not say that.

He does not know
whether the commission has to report to him or is responsible to him. May I ask this question: Is the chairman of the new radio commission in control of the minister? I think that is a fair question. The minister says he does not know. Who is head of the radio commission? Who is head of the broadcasting in this country? Is it the chairman of the commission or is it the minister?
Supply-Marine-Radio

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: It is the minister in his capacity as minister, together with the radio commission under the powers conferred upon them by the act.
Are you satisfied?
No, far from it; in fact I am rather perplexed. With all due deference I would suggest to the minister that he let this item stand and sleep on it, and tell us to-morrow who is in charge.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Perhaps in the meantime my hon. friend might read the act and become posted on the actual situation. There are some powers that are exercised by the commission, who report to the minister, and in other respects they may be under the control of the minister.
Does the minister report to the chairman of the commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
My hon. friend is
joking. The minister has no report to make to the commission. The commission reports to the minister, as I have already told the committee.

May I ask the minister whether the actual relationship between the commission and the department is not somewhat similar to the relationship between the pension commission and the Department of Pensions and National Health?
Once when I was at Sunday school-
Oh, oh.

I observe with pain the frivolous reception which greeted that remark; it indicates the low mentality of those responsible for it. As I was saying, once at Sunday school I read a beautiful little book, into the details of which I will not go now; which was called "Alone, Yet Not Alone." That seems to describe the relationship between the minister and the commission.
Now that I have a chance, Mr. Chairman- for which I have been waiting patiently for an hour and a half-I should like to ask several questions for the sake of information, which I will put together so that the minister can answer them all at once. Possibly they do not come under this item, though I think they do. I should like to know which branch of the service, that is, the radio commission or the departmental officials, is charged with the issuing of licences for radio receiving sets. Then I should like to know the system now in vogue in connection with those licences. I remember that once we went to some gov-

ernment office, but more recently we have gone to the radio agent who sold the machine and obtained our licence from him. Perhaps he received a little rake-off or commission on those licences, and if so I would like to know what it amounted to. Now it appears that they are going to have it thrown into politics, as usual, and there will be one man appointed through political influence, which has happened already in my district. He will be termed the inspector of radio licences. Pretty soon we will have an inspector of drag licences, I suppose. I must say, however, that in the district I represent a very worthy man has been selected as chief inspector, and if my memory is not wrong-and I speak subject to correction-he gets a commission of ten per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Is .that Mr. McDonald ?

For once Mr. McDonald
seems to have missed a job, but I have no doubt 'he will get the local appointment; I have every confidence in my hon. friend seeing that Mr. McDonald will get it. I understand, as I say, that the inspector gets a commission, of ten per cent. Then there is to be a local man appointed by the patronage committee in every little centre, who will have charge of the actual issuing of licences, and if I am not mistaken he will get a commission of 25 per cent. That is a total commission of 35 per cent, representing 70 cents out of the fee of S2. I do not know any tax in Canada the cost of collecting which amounts to 35 per cent.
Better look up the facts.

I asked the minister to correct me if I am wrong, and I must say perhaps I am wrong about the 25 per cent, because I do not know. But if that is so, that is a tremendous cost for collecting these amounts.
Then there is just one other point on which I should like to get information, and I hope the minister will reassure me. We know that under the old system of control we paid SI for these licences, but as soon as there was any suggestion of government control the fee was immediately jumped to S2, an increase of one hundred per cent. To a great many people the difference between $1 and $2 does not amount to anything, but to a great many more people it does mean a great deal. Now I see some symptoms, having a mean and suspicious mind, which I interpret as a sort of kite flying to see whether the people will stand for a fee of S3. I saw a suggestion recently in the Press that no doubt when the thing was working satisfactorily the people would not grudge paying S3 for such a valu-

Supply-Marine-Radio
able service. As I say, in a great many cases S3 is a very substantial item, and to many poor people living in the country whose only communication with the outer world is the radio a S3 fee will mean that the radio will have to be done without. I hope the minister will reassure me and say that the government or the commission, whichever is dominant, has no intention for this year at least of increasing the license fee beyond $2.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: The collection of radio licence fees was made last year just as it had been made previously except that on July 1, three months after the beginning of the fiscal year, we appointed inspectors to go from house to house and ascertain those who had radio licences and those who had not. These inspectors were authorized to issue lioenoeis to those who did not possess them, and they were paid a certain commission.
How much?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Forty cents per licence; we did not pay a cent more than that. I am glad my hon. friend has brought up the matter so that I may give this information to the committee and to the house. As a matter of fact the net revenue collected by the department and turned over to the Receiver General on acooumt of licences issued during the ten months ending January 31, 1933, amounted to $1,396,447.57. After estimating the number of unissued licences remainiing in the hands of dealers these figures represent approximately 735,000 licences actually issued to January 31, 1933. The distribution and sale of licences for that ten months period was as follows: 69-9 per oenit or 513,776 licences were sold by dealers, at a cost of 71 per cent.
What percentage is paid the dealer?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
He is paid 15 cents
per licence, which is at the rate of 7i per cent, and of the 735,000 licences issued, 513,776 were sold by dealers at that commission.
How much does that amount to?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
69-9 per cent of the
total for the ten months. The licences issued by the post offices numbered 130,535, or 17 per cent, and the commission paid was 2^ per cent or 5 cents per licence.

Why the difference in the
commission paid to the post offices and to other people?

What
was the total commission paid out under these three schemes?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I am just giving the figures. To answer my hon. friend in the far corner I would state that the commission paid to the post offices is less because these officials are already paid by the government. It is verry convenient to the taxpayers to be able to obtain their licences at the post offices, and this service costs the department only 5 cents per licence.
Mr. VEN'IOT:	How many radio licences
were sold by the banks?

In our district
the mounted police issue the licences.

speakerposition: Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
The sexton does it in
some places.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: The number of licences issued by the banks was 18,391 at a commission of 15 cents.

Would a bank in a town
be authorized to issue licences at a 15 cent commission when it is situated within a hundred yards of a post office?

speakerposition: Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Why pay more to a
bank than to a post office?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: We do this in order to provide every convenience for the taxpayer in buying his licence. When, a citizen goes to a bank he is able to buy his licence.

speakerposition: Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Why pay more to a
bank than to a post office?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I have already given the reason; because the postmaster is already paid by the state.

speakerposition: Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
The banks make more
money than the post offices.

Why should a bank be
authorized to issue licences at a 15 cent commission when it is situated within only fifty yards of a post office which receives only 5 cents? The minister says that the postmaster is already paid by the government, but the government would be saving money by taking this privilege away from the banks. God knows, they have enough privileges now.

How
much was paid out in commissions to these various collecting agencies?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I was giving the
figures.

Give him a chance to
answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
In answer to the
question asked by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Veniot) I would say that

four thousand small post offices are paid 15 cents per licence, the same as the banks. We do not allow all 'banks to issue licences; I am informed by the officials that this is done only when the bank is some distance away from the post office. I should like to know the place which my hon. friend has in mind.

It is Bathurst. The bank
is situated within fifty yards of the post office and contains a notice "Radio licences sold here."

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I will take note of
that and we will see that some redress is made. From July 1 last the licences issued by our inspectors numbered 84,870 or 11 per cent. The Department of Marine received the fees direct for 15,083 licences or 2 per cent. The mounted police collected for 6,896 licences.
What rake-off do they get?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I am told that so far the mounted police have received no commission.
They should all be collected by the mounted police.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I am told that the
same commission paid to the inspectors, 40 cents per licence, is paid into their retirement fund.

Are they not paid by the
state?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: They have to go from house to house, sometimes travelling miles in their own cars, in order to issue licences.
Are they not paid by the state the same as the postmasters? Why should they get a bigger percentage?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Because they have to go from house to house like the inspectors. This commission does not go to them personally, it goes to their retirement fund.

Are they not being paid by
the government while they are going from house to house? Why should the mounted police receive anything extra when they are being paid by the government?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I suppose the matter was weighed and it was thought advisable that it should be done.
Who authorized this payment, the minister or the commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: The payment would be authorized by order in council.

I am like the member for
Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot),I am disappointed. I do not think the minister was quite fair in the argument he put forth. I wanted to know what arrangements had been made for paying men in the future, and I instanced cases where political appointments had been made. The minister came back by entirely begging the question. He said that 69 per cent of the licences were issued by dealers, but does he think we are so simple that we do not know that for the most part radio licences are taken out in the spring? These political appointments were made as late as October and possibly November, and the minister tries to draw a red herring across the trail by saying that the dealers had issued 69 per cent of the licences. The discussion is on the item of fees for radio licences. The minister would then have no difficulties in collection. The manufacturers would pay the tax just the same as they do the sales tax, and every cent of the revenue would come into the treasury. I was not suggesting that everyone should go to the post office to get his licence. We have the mail carriers who go into every home and who know where every radio is located. If those carriers received a small commission you would get the finest collection system yet devised. I might go further and say to the minister that I do not believe the present system is good, speaking politically; I think it will cause more enemies than friends.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Our only aiim has
been to collect every licence fee, and I can tell my hon. friend that at the present time we are corresponding with the Post Office Department in order to see if collections cannot be made by carriers.

Some years ago, before
radio was invented, I was interested in the marketing of phonographs. When this device for reproducing music came into use I felt that the government was missing an opportunity to obtain revenue by placing a small and reasonable tax upon phonograph records. It was never necessary to have a licence to . use a phonograph and, as the minister has pointed out, it would have been utterly impossible to follow all trades engaged in the production of musical instruments. I think the minister's explanation shows that he is running into the very same problem in connection with radio receiving sets. To-day the government needs money worse than it ever did, and this afternoon the Minister of Finance stated quite frankly that he would welcome suggestions for revenue. The government has gone to a great deal of expense and yet in my opinion $125,000 is being thrown away in collecting a tax which could be collected without a cent of cost. I suggest to the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Marine that phonograph records could bear a fairly substantial tax. We pay 8 cents on a package of cigarettes; why should not phonograph records bear a fair tax? It would be a justifiable tax and would provide considerable revenue. A tax upon radio receiving sets is just as much a nuisance as a tax upon sewing machines would be; both are almost household necessities. The most equitable way of levying this tax would be to base the tax upon the use made of the machine. The man who buys an eight tube set in order to obtain 
better reception should pay more than the man who is satisfied with a four tube set. The man who uses his receiving set more than another should pay more in the way of taxation. A gasoline tax is based upon the amount of gasoline used, which represents the use made of our highways, and the same principle could be applied to this tax. By placing a 50 cent tax upon each radio tube, according to the figures for last year the government would receive a revenue of $1,600,000. There would be a great saving in the cost of collection, the whole matter would be simplified, and I believe the radio receiving set owner would be more satisfied with the general conditions. Many men occupy summer homes in which they have radio sets which are operated for probably only two months in the year. Some people take their sets back to their winter home, while others, having duplicate sets, pay for two licences. The mm who does this buys two licences but he is not living in two houses at the same time. If the tubes were taxed a man would be justified in moving the tubes, but when the tubes were worn out he would have to buy new ones upon which a tax would be imposed. This tax could be collected by the manufacturers without any cost to the government, in the same way that sales tax is collected. I submit to the minister tihait he should take up this matter with his colleagues, because I think it would prove to be in the interest of revenue, of convenience, and of economy in collection.
